newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan policymaker says HK ballot "a big joke".
newsitem.headline: Taiwan policymaker says HK ballot "a big joke".

text.p: A top Taiwan policymaker for China relations said Hong Kong's historic meeting convened by Beijing to choose the territory's future leader was "a big joke" in democracy, local media reported on Saturday.
"It is a big joke to call the election democratic," said Kao Koong-lian, deputy chairman of Taiwan's Mainland Affairs Council which sets guidelines for the island's policy toward China.
Only 400 of Hong Kong's 6.3 million people are participating in the voting for their future Chief Executive, having joined a special Selection Committee set up under China's close supervision.
The British colony returns to Chinese rule on July 1, 1997.
"The election did not meet democratic procedures in modern countries," Kao was quoted by the Central Daily News newspaper, owned by Taiwan's ruling Nationalist Party, as saying.

China's Foreign Minister Qian Qichen made his first official visit to Hong Kong on Friday to inaugurate the selection caucus, calling the committee's activities the beginning of genuine democracy in Hong Kong.
"The world is confused by communist China's election procedure," Kao said.
Taiwan, separated from China by a civil war in 1949, maintains an official policy of reunification with China, but says that reunification can only be realised when China becomes democratic.
"The whole world, especially Taiwan, is looking at the development of Hong Kong," the China Times newspaper, one of Taiwan's two major newspapers, said in its Saturday editorial.
"This (election) is very far away from the real democracy people have desired," the editorial said.
Hong Kong's handover to China has been seen as a step closer toward the future reunification of Taiwan and China -- both say they want reunification, but under very different terms.
Hong Kong's 400-member Selection Committee chose on Friday three candidates to step into the shoes of colonial governor Chris Patten when British rule ends at midnight on June 30, 1997.
The Selection Committee will meet again on December 11 to pick the Chief Executive.
Hong Kong's pro-democracy lobby has attacked the selection process and refused to take part in the selection committee which they have branded as undemocratic.
